fixation.hint: A cross to look at, to settle the eyes before a stimulus.

go-no-go-cued.hint: A green or red beacon comes first and changes the rule.

flanker-ant.label: Attention networks
flanker-ant.hint: The arrows task with warning and location cues: alerting, orienting, conflict.

n-back-self-paced.label: Self-paced n-back
n-back-self-paced.hint: The same letters, but each one stays until the participant presses Continue.

neurofeedback.label: Neurofeedback
neurofeedback.hint: Pick its video in the settings. A baseline comes first and sets the threshold.

markers.label: Event names
markers.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

lines/text.label: Text
lines/text.help: What the participant reads. A new line in the box is a new line on screen.

lines/holdMs.label: Stays on screen (ms)
lines/holdMs.help: How long this line is shown before the next one. 1000 ms is one second.

lines/marker.label: Event name
lines/marker.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

lines.label: Lines of text
lines.help: Shown one after another, in this order.

advance/mode.label: The block ends
advance/mode.help: After a fixed time, when the participant presses the button, or whichever comes first.

advance/label.label: Button text
advance/label.help: What the button that moves on says, for example Continue or Start.

advance/ms.label: Duration (ms)
advance/ms.help: How long the block lasts when it ends on its own.

advance/minMs.label: Button appears after (ms)
advance/minMs.help: The button is disabled until then, so nobody skips the text without reading it.

advance/maxMs.label: Moves on by itself after (ms)
advance/maxMs.help: A time limit for a participant who never presses the button.

footnote.label: Small print
footnote.help: A quiet line under the text, for a reminder like 'you can stop at any time'.

markers/*.help: The name this moment gets in the recording's event timeline. Change it only if your analysis expects a specific name.

allowPause.label: The participant can pause
allowPause.help: Off keeps every participant on the same timeline, which is what you want when comparing them.

endOn.label: The block ends
endOn.help: When the video finishes, or after a fixed time even if the video is longer.

durationMs.label: Fixed time (ms)
durationMs.help: Only used when the block ends after a fixed time.

start_s.label: Start at (s)
start_s.help: Play from this second of the video instead of its beginning. Splitting a clip on the timeline fills this in.

end_s.label: Stop at (s)
end_s.help: Stop at this second of the video instead of its end.

cues.label: Moments to mark
cues.help: Points in the video you want to find again in the recording: a jump scare, a scene change. Each becomes an event on the timeline.

cues/atS.label: At (s)
cues/atS.help: Seconds from the start of the video.

cues/label.label: Name
cues/label.help: How the event is called in the timeline.

cues/note.label: Note
cues/note.help: For you; the participant never sees it.

start_s.label: Start at (s)
start_s.help: Skip the beginning of the file: play from this second.

end_s.label: Stop at (s)
end_s.help: Cut the end of the file: stop at this second.

min_s.label: Shortest reading time (s)
min_s.help: Continue is disabled until then, so the text is actually read.

eyes.label: Eyes
eyes.help: Eyes closed gives the strongest alpha rhythm and is the reference the review page compares every block to. Eyes open is closer to how the other blocks are done.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: One to two minutes is usual. Under 30 s is too short to be a stable reference.

end_tone.label: Play a tone at the end
end_tone.help: So a participant with closed eyes knows when to open them.

mode.label: The break ends
mode.help: After a fixed time, or when the participant feels ready.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: Used when the break ends after a fixed time.

message.label: Message
message.help: What the screen says during the break.

duration_s.label: Duration (s)
duration_s.help: How long the cross stays. One second or two before a stimulus is usual.

n.label: Trials
n.help: How many rows of arrows. 96 takes about three minutes; with cues use a multiple of 8 so every combination comes up equally often.

congruentRatio.label: Share of agreeing rows
congruentRatio.help: The fraction of rows whose outer arrows point the same way as the middle one, from 0 to 1. At 0.5 the disagreement cannot be predicted.

cues.label: Cues before the row
cues.help: Leave empty for the plain arrows task. With cues the row appears above or below the cross and a brief asterisk may come first: this is the Attention Network Test. Use all four for its three scores.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every trial as practice: played, never scored.

feedback.label: Say right or wrong
feedback.help: Shows Correct, Wrong side or Too slow after each row. Use it for practice; in the real block it changes how people respond.

maxRun.label: Longest streak
maxRun.help: The most rows of the same type in a row.

cueMs.label: Cue stays on (ms)
cueMs.help: 100 ms is the standard: long enough to see, too short to look at.

cueTargetMs.label: Cue to row (ms)
cueTargetMs.help: The quiet gap between the cue going off and the row appearing.

stimulusMs.label: Time to answer (ms)
stimulusMs.help: The row stays up until an answer or this long, then counts as too slow.

itiMs.label: Pause between rows (ms)
itiMs.help: Shortest and longest time on the cross between two rows. Varying it stops people answering to the rhythm.

pace.label: Pace
pace.help: Fixed: every letter gets the same time, answered or not - the standard n-back. Self-paced: each letter stays until the participant presses Continue, with Match before it; it takes away the time pressure and records how long each letter was kept.

n.label: Letters
n.help: How many letters are shown. 60 takes two and a half minutes.

load.label: How far back
load.help: 1: is it the same as the previous letter? 2: the same as the one before that? 3 is hard for most people. Compare blocks of different loads to see effort rise.

matchRatio.label: Share of matches
matchRatio.help: The fraction of letters that repeat the one from that far back, from 0 to 1. About 0.3 is standard.

lureRatio.label: Share of near misses
lureRatio.help: Letters that repeat one step off: they feel like a match and must be let go. They tell remembering the order from merely recognising a recent letter. 0 turns them off.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every trial as practice: played, never scored.

stimulusMs.label: Letter stays on (ms)
stimulusMs.help: The letter disappears after this long; the answer can still come.

isiMs.label: Blank after the letter (ms)
isiMs.help: The pace is fixed: every letter gets its time plus this blank, answered or not.

gapMs.label: Blank after Continue (ms)
gapMs.help: A short blank between letters, so two equal letters in a row read as two.

duration_s.label: Length (seconds)
duration_s.help: How long the participant keeps matching. 90 seconds is the standard; the score is how many they get right in that time.

practice.label: This is a practice round
practice.help: Marks every answer as practice: played, never scored.

pairs.label: Symbols in the key
pairs.help: How many symbol-digit pairs to look up, from 2 to 9. Nine is the standard; fewer makes it easier to memorise and less of a speed test.

itiMs.label: Pause between symbols (ms)
itiMs.help: A brief blank after each answer, so two identical-looking moments are not mistaken for one.

intervals_s.label: Counting rounds (seconds each)
intervals_s.help: One number per round. Use different lengths, or people multiply a guessed heart rate by the time. The headband's pulse sensor counts the real beats.

shuffle.label: Rounds in a random order
shuffle.help: A different order each session, so the lengths cannot be learned.

confidence.label: Ask how sure they are
confidence.help: After each round. How well confidence follows accuracy is its own measure, and the more telling one in anxiety.

ready_s.label: Get-ready time (seconds)
ready_s.help: How long the instruction is shown before the starting tone.

inhaleMs.label: Breathe in (ms)
inhaleMs.help: How long the circle grows. 4500 ms with the same out is about 6.5 breaths a minute.

holdMs.label: Hold (ms)
holdMs.help: A pause between in and out. Leave empty for none.

lines.label: Text after the breaths
lines.help: Optional lines shown one after another once the last breath ends, in place of the circle. To tell the participant what comes next, an Instructions block after this one is clearer.

variant.label: Version
variant.help: Simple: dock the blue cargo, let the orange debris pass. With a beacon: a green or red light comes first and changes the rule, which is harder.

n.label: Objects
n.help: How many objects cross the screen. 100 takes about two minutes.

goRatio.label: Share of cargo
goRatio.help: The fraction of objects to dock, from 0 to 1. Around 0.7 makes docking a habit, which is what makes holding back hard.

validGoRatio.label: Share of green beacon + cargo
validGoRatio.help: The fraction of trials where the participant should dock, from 0 to 1.

practice.label: Practice round first
practice.help: A few unscored objects before the real ones.

travelMs.label: Crossing time (ms)
travelMs.help: How long an object takes to cross the screen: a shortest and a longest time, picked at random between the two. Shorter is harder.

itiMs.label: Pause between objects (ms)
itiMs.help: Shortest and longest empty time between two objects.

cueMs.label: Beacon stays on (ms)
cueMs.help: Shortest and longest time the beacon is lit.

cueTargetMs.label: Beacon to object (ms)
cueTargetMs.help: Shortest and longest wait between the beacon and the object.

maxRun.label: Most cargo in a row
maxRun.help: Keeps the random order from producing long streaks that make the task predictable.

maxNogoRun.label: Most debris in a row
maxNogoRun.help: Same, for the objects to let pass.

maxCueRun.label: Most same beacons in a row
maxCueRun.help: Limits streaks of the same beacon colour.

maxOutcomeRun.label: Most same answers in a row
maxOutcomeRun.help: Limits streaks of trials with the same right answer.

nogoMix.label: Kinds of 'hold' trials
nogoMix.help: How the trials where the participant must not dock are split. The three shares add up to 1.

items.label: Images
items.help: Shown in this order, or shuffled.

items/id.label: Name
items/id.help: How this image is called in the timeline.

items/class.label: Category
items/class.help: A group the image belongs to (faces, houses), for comparing categories later.

jitterMs.label: Random extra gap (ms)
jitterMs.help: Up to this much is added to each gap, so the rhythm is not predictable.

shuffle.label: Shuffle the order
shuffle.help: A different order per participant, the same for the same participant and seed.

instrument.label: Questionnaire
instrument.help: SAM asks how pleasant and how activated the participant feels, with pictures. VAS is a single slider. NASA-TLX measures workload. Custom uses your own questions below.

prompt.label: Question on top
prompt.help: Shown above the scales, for example 'How did the video make you feel?'

items.label: Your questions
items.help: Only used by the Custom questionnaire.

items/id.label: Short name
items/id.help: How the answer is called in the exported data.

scenes/correct.label: Right answer (number)
scenes/correct.help: The position of the right answer in the list, starting from 0.

feedback.label: Say if the answer was right
feedback.help: Off keeps the participant from learning during the quiz.

signal.label: Brain rhythm
signal.help: What the feedback follows, measured in the browser from the headband. A band is its share of all the power between 1 and 45 Hz; a ratio divides one band by the other.

options.landscape_region: A place of the person's landscape

feedback.label: What the person watches
feedback.help: The video below, or a built-in animation that needs no media: a plane that takes off in target, two notes that come into tune, or the two ribbons of light coming into focus. Or a game, Lantern: the signal is the light on a path, the hands choose each fork.

direction.label: Reward when the value is
direction.help: Above or below the threshold. Left empty, theta, beta and theta/beta are trained down and the others up.

channels.label: Electrodes
channels.help: Left empty, theta and theta/beta are read on the forehead (AF7, AF8) and the others behind the ears (TP9, TP10): at the forehead, beta and SMR are mostly the muscle above the eyebrows.

effect.label: The picture
effect.help: Brightness only, or brightness plus a blur that clears in target.

duration_s.label: Training time (seconds)
duration_s.help: How long the feedback runs after the baseline. Up to 30 minutes; long blocks tire people.

baseline_s.label: Baseline (seconds)
baseline_s.help: The video at a steady brightness while the signal is measured; it sets the threshold. 0 for none, which needs a fixed threshold.

threshold/mode.label: Threshold from
threshold/mode.help: From this person's baseline today, a fixed number that stays the same across sessions, or carried: the threshold the run's previous neurofeedback block on the same signal ended on, with no baseline (the first such block runs its baseline). Carry is for games in rounds.

threshold/target_fraction.label: Share of the baseline in target
threshold/target_fraction.help: 0.4 sets the threshold so that 40% of the baseline would have been rewarded.

threshold/value.label: Fixed threshold
threshold/value.help: A share between 0 and 1 for a band (0.25 is a quarter of the power), or the ratio itself.

game/start_level.label: Starting level

alpha.meaning: Share of the signal's power in the 8–12 Hz band. It rises when you relax with eyes closed and drops when you look and pay attention.

beta.name: Beta
beta.meaning: Share of power in the 13–30 Hz band. It tends to rise with alert, focused or tense activity.

theta.name: Theta
theta.meaning: Share of power in the 4–8 Hz band. It rises with drowsiness, and at the front of the head with effortful focus and memory.

delta.name: Delta
delta.meaning: Share of power below 4 Hz. Awake, much of it comes from movement and blinks, so a high value often means a noisier stretch.

entropy.name: Entropy
entropy.meaning: How hard it is to guess the next brain state from the current one, in bits. Low: the signal follows a routine; high: it wanders unpredictably.

recurrence.name: Recurrence
recurrence.meaning: How often a move goes back to a state already visited in this stretch. High: the signal circles familiar places; low: it keeps finding new ones.

modularity.name: Modularity
modularity.meaning: How much windows of the same kind of trial gather in the same states. Near 0: kinds of trial mix freely; higher: each has places of its own.

diameter.name: Diameter
diameter.meaning: How wide the range of brain states covered is, in ball widths of the map. Larger: the signal ranged further.

stretching.name: Stretching
stretching.meaning: The average step from one moment to the next, as a share of the diameter. High: big jumps across the space; low: small, gradual drift.

accuracy.name: Right actions
accuracy.meaning: Share of trials where the person did what the task asked. Read it with false alarms: pressing less can raise it on its own.

reaction_time.name: Reaction time
reaction_time.meaning: Typical time from the target appearing to the press (the median). Lower is faster.

rt_spread.name: Reaction spread
rt_spread.meaning: How much the reaction time varied from trial to trial. Lower is steadier.

hit_rate.name: Targets caught
hit_rate.meaning: Share of targets that got an answer. Missed targets pull it down.

false_alarms.name: False alarms
false_alarms.meaning: Share of non-targets pressed anyway: acting before checking. Lower is more careful.

privacy.title: What happens to your data.
privacy.draft: Brain Trails is a non-clinical research prototype, and this note is a draft published pending legal review. It describes what the system actually does today. It will be replaced by a reviewed policy, and we will tell you when that happens.
privacy.intro: Protecting the privacy of the people who use Brain Trails matters to us more than anything else we do with this prototype — we are asking you for recordings of your brain, and we do not take that lightly. We are making every effort to keep your data secure and to bring this note fully in line with the law that applies to it. We have tried hard to describe only what is true today rather than what we intend to build, and where something is not built yet, this note says so.

whatItIs.title: 1. What Brain Trails is, and is not
whatItIs.p1: Brain Trails is provided for informational and wellness purposes. Unless Lumentis Analytics Inc. says otherwise in writing, it is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, prevent or monitor any disease or medical condition. It does not provide medical advice.
whatItIs.p2: Do not make medical decisions based on it. Talk to a qualified health-care professional about symptoms, diagnosis or treatment.

whoWeAre.title: 2. Who we are
whoWeAre.p1: Lumentis Analytics Inc. is responsible for the personal information processed through Brain Trails.
whoWeAre.addressee: Lumentis Analytics Inc., Attn: Privacy Officer
whoWeAre.postalAddress: 329 Howe Street, Unit 272, Vancouver, British Columbia V6C 3N2, Canada

collect.title: 3. What we collect
collect.p1: Your account. Your email address, your password (stored only as a hash, never as text we can read), and an account identifier we generate.
collect.p2: What you tell us about yourself. Your name, year of birth and handedness, and — if you choose to give them — details such as sex at birth, sleep, caffeine, medications, and neurological or psychiatric conditions. Several of these are health-related and sensitive. Only the few that make a recording interpretable are required, none of them at sign-up, and the rest are offered and never demanded.
collect.p3: Your recordings. The EEG captured during a session, signal-quality and device information, your responses and timings during an exercise, and everything derived from them: features, metrics, projections, visualisations and reports.
collect.p4: EEG recordings and what we derive from them may be sensitive personal information. Depending on the context they may be treated as health-related or biometric information.
collect.p5: Technical information. Ordinary server logs, browser and device type, IP address, and the session cookie that keeps you signed in.

use.title: 4. What we do with it
use.p1: We use it to run the service: to keep your account, to receive and process your recordings, to compute the analyses and reports you asked for, to show you your history, to keep the service secure and working, and to answer you when you write to us.
use.p2: Improving Brain Trails itself. We use recordings and derived data to check and improve the accuracy and reliability of what Brain Trails does — whether a reading is sound, whether a metric behaves, why something failed. This is part of running the service you are using.
use.p3: Broader research — only if you say yes. Separately, and only with the optional consent you can give at sign-up and change at any time on your account page, we may keep and use your pseudonymised recordings and derived data for scientific research going beyond running and improving this service. Saying no changes nothing about your account, your recordings or your results. If you withdraw, we stop using your data for research from that point; we cannot undo research already done, or recover data that has been irreversibly anonymised.
use.p4: We do not sell your personal information, your recordings or anything derived from them, and we do not use them for advertising or behavioural tracking of any kind.

consent.title: 5. Consent
consent.p1: We ask for two things separately. The first is consent to process your recordings and account data in order to provide Brain Trails at all — without it there is no service to give you. The second is the optional research consent above.
consent.p2: You can withdraw the optional one at any time from your account page. You can withdraw the first by deleting your account, also from your account page, or by writing to us. Withdrawing does not undo processing already carried out.

pseudonymised.title: 6. Pseudonymised is not anonymous
pseudonymised.p1: Your recordings and everything derived from them are stored against a randomly generated identifier rather than your name or your email, and the files themselves carry no identifying detail in their names or their contents. Your identity lives in a separate database.
pseudonymised.p2: That is a real protection, and it is not anonymity. While we can reconnect an identifier to you — and through our own account system, we can — the data is still personal information, and this note treats it as such throughout. We will not describe anything as anonymous unless it has been processed so that a person is no longer reasonably identifiable from it.

storage.title: 7. Where it is stored
storage.p1: Lumentis Analytics Inc. is a Canadian company. Recordings, files and the application database are stored in Frankfurt, Germany. The application itself is served by Vercel, whose network is global, so requests may be handled outside that region even though the data at rest is not.
storage.p2: Authorised Lumentis personnel may access the data from Canada and Italy, where necessary to run, maintain and support the service.

security.title: 8. Security
security.p1: Some of what protects your data comes from the platforms we build on, by default and without us configuring anything:

platforms.1: Files are encrypted at rest. Amazon S3 applies AES-256 server-side encryption to every new object as a baseline that cannot be switched off (<link>AWS documents this</link>).
platforms.2: The database is encrypted at rest and reached over TLS; see <link>Neon’s security overview</link>.
platforms.3: Traffic between your browser and us travels over HTTPS.

security.p2: And some of it is our own doing:

own.1: Passwords are stored only as Argon2 hashes. We cannot read them.
own.2: Your files are never public. They are reached through links that are generated for one file and expire within minutes.
own.3: Access to the systems holding recordings is limited to the small number of people who run the service.
own.4: Identity is kept in a different place from the recordings, as described in section 6.

security.p3: Linking to those pages tells you what our providers do; it is not a claim that everything on our side is configured perfectly. No system is completely secure, and we cannot promise that yours will never be breached. What we can promise is that we will investigate anything we suspect and tell you where the law requires it — and, for something this sensitive, where it does not but you would obviously want to know.

retention.title: 9. Keeping it, and deleting it
retention.p1: We keep your account and your recordings while your account exists and this prototype is running. We have not set a fixed retention period yet and we are not going to invent one here: you can export or delete everything yourself, at any time, from your account page.
retention.p2: Because this is a prototype, data may also be removed when we reset an environment. We will give you notice before doing that deliberately.
retention.p3: When you delete your account, we delete your personal information: your recordings and the files behind them, the analyses and reports derived from them, your profile — including any health-related answers you gave — and the account itself.
retention.p4: One narrow exception. We keep a minimal record that consent was given and later withdrawn or deleted, so that we can show we asked properly and honoured your request. That record contains no EEG data, no health information, no name and no email address — only an account identifier, which version of this note was agreed to, and when. Once your account is deleted, that identifier no longer points to anything we hold.
retention.p5: Backups are not edited by hand. Copies of data held in backups disappear as those backups expire on their normal cycle.

disclosure.title: 10. Who else sees it
disclosure.p1: We do not sell your personal information and we do not share it for advertising. It is disclosed only to the providers who host and run the service on our behalf under contract — today our cloud storage, database, hosting and email providers — to professional advisers where genuinely necessary, where the law or a valid legal process requires it, to protect people from harm, in connection with a business transaction subject to privacy law, and to anyone you ask us to share it with.

rights.title: 11. Your rights
rights.p1: Two of these you can exercise yourself, right now, from your account page: export everything we hold about you, and delete your account. You can also grant or withdraw the optional research consent there.
rights.p2: For anything else — access, correction, restricting or objecting to particular processing, or asking what we have disclosed — write to <email>{privacyEmail}</email>. A person reads that address. We may need to confirm who you are before we act.
rights.p3: If you are not satisfied with how we have handled something, you can complain to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, or to the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia.

cookies.title: 12. Cookies
cookies.p1: We use one cookie, to keep you signed in, and browser storage for small preferences such as whether you chose the light or the dark theme. No advertising cookies, no third-party analytics, no tracking pixels. If you block the session cookie you will not be able to sign in.
cookies.p2: A session cookie or a stored identifier does not make your recordings anonymous. If an identifier lets us find your data, that data is still personal information.

age.title: 13. Age
age.p1: Brain Trails is for people aged 18 and over. We do not knowingly open accounts for anyone younger. If you believe someone under 18 has created an account, write to us and we will delete it.

otherServices.title: 14. Other services
otherServices.p1: Brain Trails works with a Muse EEG headband, which is made and supported by another company under its own privacy policy. The same goes for the infrastructure providers named above. We encourage you to read their notices.

changes.title: 15. Changes to this note
changes.p1: When we change this note in a way that matters, we will publish a new version and ask you to read and agree to it the next time you sign in. The version is at the top of this page and is recorded against your account when you agree, so there is always a record of what you actually agreed to.

contact.title: 16. Contact
contact.p1: Questions, requests or complaints: <email>{privacyEmail}</email>, or Lumentis Analytics Inc., Attn: Privacy Officer, 329 Howe Street, Unit 272, Vancouver, British Columbia V6C 3N2, Canada.

attention-networks.title: Attention Networks
attention-networks.summary: The arrows game with warning flashes: alerting, orienting and conflict, separately.
attention-networks.description: The Attention Network Test. A flash may warn you that the arrows are coming, or show you where; the arrows may agree or not. Comparing those cases gives three scores: how much a warning helps, how much knowing the place helps, and what conflict costs. Two rounds of four minutes.
attention-networks.contentWarning: Arrows and brief flashes appear on the screen for about eight minutes, and you answer quickly. You can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then two rounds of a game with arrows.

1.text: About twelve minutes in all.

0.text:
Keep your eyes on the cross.
A row of arrows will appear above or below it.

1.text:
Which way does the MIDDLE arrow point?
Press the left or right arrow key, or tap the side.

2.text:
Sometimes a star flashes first. It tells you the arrows are coming,
and sometimes where. Keep looking at the cross.

3.text: A short practice first. It will tell you how you did.

0.text:
That was practice.
Now two rounds of four minutes, with a break between.

config.message: Rest your eyes. Round two starts by itself.

0.text: All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

breath-pacing.title: Breath Pacing
breath-pacing.summary: Five minutes of slow breathing, six breaths a minute, between two rests.
breath-pacing.description: Breathe in for four seconds and out for six, following a circle. Rest before and after with your eyes closed, and say how you feel each time, so the change has two ends. With a headband that has a pulse sensor your heart rate is measured along.

0.text: First you rest, then you breathe with a circle for five minutes.

1.text: About nine minutes in all.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text:
Breathe in as the circle grows,
out as it shrinks.

1.text:
Out is longer than in. Let it be easy:
if you feel light-headed, breathe normally.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel now.

0.text: All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

emotion-video.title: Emotion video
emotion-video.summary: Short film clips in random order, each followed by how it made you feel.
emotion-video.description: A resting baseline, then cleared film clips in an order drawn for this session, each followed by a rest and a Self-Assessment Manikin, then a closing baseline.
emotion-video.contentWarning: This protocol shows short film clips chosen to evoke emotions, some of them unpleasant. You can stop at any time.

config.prompt: Think of how you felt while watching the clip.

flanker-control.title: Flanker Control
flanker-control.summary: Which way does the middle arrow point, when the ones around it disagree?
flanker-control.description: A row of five arrows, answered as fast as you can. When the outer arrows point the other way you slow down and slip more often: that cost is how hard your attention works to shut out what is next to the target, and your brain's response to a slip is measured too.
flanker-control.contentWarning: Arrows flash on the screen for about four minutes, and you answer quickly. You can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then a quick game with arrows.

1.text: About seven minutes in all.

0.text: A row of arrows will appear.

1.text:
Which way does the MIDDLE arrow point?
Press the left or right arrow key, or tap the side.

2.text:
The other arrows may point the other way. Ignore them.
Be fast, but be right.

3.text: A short practice first. It will tell you how you did.

0.text:
That was practice.
Now about four minutes, without the hints.
All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

free-recording.title: Free recording
free-recording.summary: Record your EEG with nothing on screen, for as long as you like.
free-recording.description: No stimulus: the headband records while you rest, read or meditate, and you stop when you are done. The simplest way to see your own trail.

interoceptive-focus.title: Interoceptive Focus
interoceptive-focus.summary: Count your own heartbeats between two tones, without touching your pulse.
interoceptive-focus.description: Four rounds of silent counting, then how many and how sure. The headband's pulse sensor counts the real beats, so you see how closely you feel your own heart - and whether your confidence follows your accuracy, which is the more telling part.

0.text: First you rest, then you listen for your own heartbeat, four times.

1.text: About seven minutes in all. Sit comfortably, hands resting, sound on.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text: Between two tones, silently count your heartbeats.

1.text:
Do not touch your wrist or neck. Just feel.
Count only the beats you really feel. Do not guess.

2.text: Then type how many. Feeling few or none is a normal answer.

0.text: All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

lantern-rounds.title: Lantern rounds
lantern-rounds.summary: Three rounds of a lantern game on your alpha, each followed by a rest on the screen.
lantern-rounds.description: Walk a path in the dark: the light reaches further as your alpha rises, and your hands choose each fork. Between rounds you rest your eyes on the screen, with nothing to follow, so the recording shows what you keep without the game's help.
lantern-rounds.contentWarning: A warm light that grows and dims slowly with your signal, three times for three minutes. You can stop at any time.

0.text: Three rounds: you walk a path with a lantern, then you rest your eyes on the screen.

1.text:
The calmer and more focused you are, the further the light reaches.
At each fork, press the arrow on the side of the mark.

2.text:
Keep your head still: the light sways when it moves.
About twenty minutes in all.

0.text: That's all. Your rounds are on your recording page.

processing-speed.title: Processing Speed
processing-speed.summary: Match symbols to numbers against the clock, twice for ninety seconds.
processing-speed.description: A table pairs nine symbols with nine digits; a symbol appears and you press its digit, as many as you can. One of the most sensitive short measures of mental speed there is: it moves with sleep, age and fatigue. The table changes each round.

0.text: A short rest, then two rounds of matching symbols to numbers against the clock.

1.text: About six minutes in all.

0.text: A table at the top pairs each symbol with a number.

1.text:
A symbol appears in the middle.
Press its number, on the keyboard or on the screen.

2.text: As many as you can, without mistakes. A short practice first.

0.text:
Now ninety seconds. The table has changed.
Go as fast as you can while staying right.

config.message: Shake out your hands. One more round, with a new table.

0.text: All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

resting-baseline.title: Resting baseline
resting-baseline.summary: One minute eyes open, one minute eyes closed.
resting-baseline.description: The reference every other session is compared with: two minutes at rest, first with your eyes open on a cross, then closed until a tone tells you to open them.

0.text: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop.

1.text:
First, one minute with your eyes open on a cross.
Then one minute with your eyes closed.

2.text: Keep still and relax your face and jaw.

signal-navigator.title: Signal Navigator
signal-navigator.summary: A go/no-go attention game with paced breathing.
signal-navigator.description: Dock the cargo and let the debris pass. Paced breathing first, then two rounds of the game: it measures how well you hold a rule and withhold a response.
signal-navigator.contentWarning: Objects move across the screen for about five minutes. A reduced-motion mode is available, and you can stop at any time.

0.text: Cargo will cross your screen.

1.text:
Press Dock for blue cargo.
Let debris pass.

rule.label: The rule for the next route

0.text: Notice the urge to rush.

1.text:
For the next route:
Beacon first, cargo second.

0.text: Route complete.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

sustained-focus.title: Sustained Focus
sustained-focus.summary: Six unbroken minutes of go/no-go, with resting baselines and a mood check.
sustained-focus.description: Rest with your eyes closed, practise, then dock cargo for six minutes while rare debris asks you to hold back. Built to be measured: enough trials to see your brain's response to withholding and to a slip, and long enough to see focus drift.
sustained-focus.contentWarning: Objects move across the screen for about six minutes without a break. A reduced-motion mode is available, and you can stop at any time.

0.text: First you rest, then one long route.

1.text: About nine minutes in all.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel right now.

0.text: Cargo will cross your screen.

1.text:
Press Dock for blue cargo.
Let debris pass.

0.text:
That was practice.
The route ahead is about six minutes.

1.text:
Most of it is cargo.
Stay ready for the debris.

config.prompt: Think of how you feel now that the route is over.

0.text: Route complete.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

working-memory-span.title: Working Memory Span
working-memory-span.summary: Letters one at a time: is this the one from one step back? From two?
working-memory-span.description: The n-back. Easy first, then harder: you keep the last letters in mind and update them at every new one. Frontal theta rises with the load, which is exactly where a headband listens, and you rate how hard it felt at the end.

0.text: First you rest, then a memory game with letters, easy and then harder.

1.text: About nine minutes in all.

0.text: Letters appear one at a time.

1.text:
Press Match (or the space bar) when a letter
is the SAME AS THE ONE JUST BEFORE it.

2.text: Otherwise do nothing. A short practice first.

0.text:
Now press Match when a letter is the same
as the one TWO BEFORE it.

1.text:
B ... K ... B  is a match.
B ... B is not. It is meant to be hard.

config.prompt: Think of the last round, two back.

0.text: All done.

1.text: Rest for a moment.

config.footnote: This is not a medical test or diagnosis.

evidence.title: Before you start
evidence.preset: The focus preset follows the oldest neurofeedback protocol for ADHD, theta/beta down, measured on your own recordings. It says where you were most focused in your own terms, nothing about anyone else.
evidence.studies: The evidence is mixed: some studies found benefits, the largest blinded trials and reviews found none beyond placebo. Theta/beta is not a reliable marker of ADHD.
evidence.delay: Your position comes from the analysis of each second of signal and arrives about one to two seconds late: the feedback follows states you hold, not single moments.

intro.title: Encoding: a picture in a few numbers
intro.body:
This is a heartbeat, as an electrocardiogram (ECG) draws it. On a screen it is hundreds of dots. Yet a doctor can describe it in a few words, and a computer in a few numbers.

Encoding means choosing a recipe that turns something into a short list of numbers (its code). Decoding means using the same recipe backwards, to rebuild the thing from its code.

At every step we will ask the same three questions: how many numbers do we need, what are their values, and how do we rebuild the picture from them?

line.title: A point on a line
line.body:
We start with the simplest picture there is: a dot on a ruler. Look at the nine pictures below. What changes from one to the next?

Only the position of the dot. So one number is enough to describe any of these pictures: how far along the ruler the dot is. We call it x.

plane.title: A point on a plane
plane.body:
Now the dot can move left and right and up and down. One number is no longer enough: two dots can share the same x and still be in different places.

We need two numbers, x and y, the coordinates you know from maths. Each number answers one question: how far right, how far up.

bellPosition.title: A bell that moves
bellPosition.body:
Now the pictures are curves: a gaussian bell, the shape of so many things in nature (heights in a class, errors of a measurement).

A curve is drawn with hundreds of dots, but look: in these nine pictures the bells are all the same, only shifted. So we still need one number: where the top of the bell is. We call it μ (mu, the centre).

This is the big idea of encoding: the number of numbers depends on what changes, not on how complicated the picture looks.

bellHeight.title: A bell that moves and grows
bellHeight.body:
Now the bells also have different heights. A second number is needed: the height of the top, A (for amplitude).

The code of each picture is now two numbers, μ and A: the same count as a point on a plane. In fact, every bell here is a point on a plane whose axes are μ and A.

bellWidth.title: A bell that moves, grows and spreads
bellWidth.body:
Last ingredient: the bells now have different widths. The width is called σ (sigma, the spread). A small σ makes a thin spike, a large σ a wide hill.

Three numbers, μ, A and σ, describe any bell. The recipe to decode them is the formula A · e^(−(x − μ)² / 2σ²): for every x, compute it, and draw the dot.

Try it below: move the three numbers until your bell sits on the dashed one.

waves.title: Waves
waves.body:
A new family: sine waves, the shape of sound, light and of many rhythms of the brain.

Two numbers change here. The frequency f: how many full waves fit in one second. The amplitude A: how high the wave goes. A cosine is the same wave shifted a little: if we wanted to allow that shift we would add a third number, the phase.

train.title: Bells in a row
train.body:
Now we put bells one after the other, at a regular distance, like the beats of a drum.

Each picture needs three numbers: the height A of the bells, their width σ and the frequency f, how many bells per second. We do not need the position of every bell: the frequency gives them all at once. A good recipe lets a few numbers say a lot.

twoBells.title: A bell up, a bell down
twoBells.body:
In every beat we now add a second bell with a minus sign: it points down. The beat gets the shape of a small wave going up and then down.

The code grows: the frequency f, the first bell's height and width (A₁, σ₁), the second bell's height and width (A₂, negative, and σ₂), and how long after the first the second comes (d).

ecg.title: A heartbeat
ecg.body:
We have everything we need for a real signal. One heartbeat on an ECG is made of waves with names: P (the top chambers of the heart squeeze), Q, R, S (the big chambers squeeze: the sharp spike), T (they relax), and a tiny U.

Each of these waves is well described by a bell, some up and some down, some thin and some wide. With eight bells the beat is almost perfect. Switch them on and off below to see which bump each one draws.

eeg.title: And now... the brain
eeg.body:
This is an EEG: the electrical activity of the brain, as the headband records it from the scalp.

Look at it for a moment. Where are the bells? Where are the waves? There is no beat that repeats, no shape we can name. We do not know the recipe. So how can we choose how many numbers to use, and how to rebuild the signal from them?

vae.title: Let a machine find the recipe
vae.body:
When we do not know the recipe, we can let a computer learn it from many examples. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is made of two neural networks: an encoder, which turns a piece of EEG into a few numbers, and a decoder, which rebuilds the EEG from those numbers.

It is exactly what we did all along: we choose how many numbers (here, eight), the encoder finds their values, the decoder rebuilds. The difference is that nobody writes the recipe: the two networks are trained together, on thousands of examples, until what comes out looks like what went in.

And the bells come back: in a VAE each number is not a single value but a small bell (a centre μ and a spread σ), so that close codes rebuild similar signals. Brain Trails uses a network of this family to turn every few seconds of your EEG into a list of numbers: your trail is drawn from them.

recap.title: Recap
recap.body: Encoding always takes the same three decisions: a recipe (a point, a bell, a wave, a row of bells, a network), how many numbers it needs, and how to decode them back. A good code is short and still rebuilds the picture well.

introWhy.prompt: What would be the most useful way to send this heartbeat to a doctor's computer?

options.pixels: The colour of every dot of the screen
options.numbers: A few numbers that describe its shape

introWhy.explain: A few numbers. The dots take a lot of space and say nothing about the shape; a sentence cannot be used to draw the beat again. A short code that can be decoded back into the picture is the best of both.

lineCount.prompt: How many numbers do you need to describe one of these pictures?
lineCount.explain: One: the position x of the dot along the line. Everything else (the line, the ticks) is the same in every picture, so it belongs to the recipe, not to the code.

lineValue.prompt: Encode this picture: what is its x?
lineValue.explain: The dot is halfway between 6 and 7, so x = 6.5. Reading the value of a picture is the encoding step.

lineDecode.prompt: Someone sends you the code x = 3. Put the steps to rebuild the picture in order.

steps.axis: Draw the line with its ticks from 0 to 10

lineDecode.explain: First the parts that never change (the recipe), then the code tells you where the only thing that changes goes. That is decoding.

planeCount.prompt: How many numbers for a point on the plane?
planeCount.explain: Two: x (how far right) and y (how far up). With only one, you could not tell apart two points one above the other.

planeMatch.prompt: Encode: drop each picture onto its code.
planeMatch.explain: Read x on the horizontal axis and y on the vertical one. Each pair of numbers is one and only one place on the plane.

bellPositionCount.prompt: These curves are made of hundreds of dots. How many numbers do you need to describe one of them?
bellPositionCount.explain: Just one, the centre μ: the bells are all identical apart from where they are. What counts is how many things change.

bellPositionSort.prompt: Sort these bells from the smallest μ to the largest.
bellPositionSort.explain: μ is where the top is: the further right, the larger μ. Sorting pictures by a number is a way of reading their code.

bellHeightCount.prompt: Now the bells move and change height. How many numbers?
bellHeightCount.explain: Two: the centre μ and the height A.

bellHeightMatch.prompt: Drop each bell onto its code.
bellHeightMatch.explain: μ is where the top is, A how high it goes. Two bells in the same place but with different heights have different codes.

bellWidthCount.prompt: Centre, height and width all change. How many numbers?
bellWidthCount.explain: Three: μ, A and σ. Every possible bell is one point in a space with three axes.

bellWidthSort.prompt: Same centre, same height. Sort them from the smallest σ to the largest.
bellWidthSort.explain: σ is the spread: the thinnest bell has the smallest σ, the widest hill the largest.

bellDecode.prompt: You receive the code μ = 6, A = 1.5, σ = 0.7. Put the steps to rebuild the bell in order.

steps.read: Read the three numbers of the code
steps.centre: Put the top of the bell at x = 6
steps.spread: Open the sides so that the bell is 0.7 wide on each side of the centre

bellDecode.explain: Decoding a bell: centre, height, spread. A computer does all three at once with the formula A · e^(−(x − μ)² / 2σ²).

wavesCount.prompt: How many numbers does each of these waves need?
wavesCount.explain: Two: the frequency f and the amplitude A. All these waves start at zero going up, so we do not need the phase.

wavesValue.prompt: Encode this wave: what are its f and A? (The axis is in seconds.)
wavesValue.explain: In one second there are two full waves, so f = 2; the top reaches 1.5, so A = 1.5.

wavesMatch.prompt: Drop each wave onto its code.
wavesMatch.explain: Count the waves in one second for f, look at how high they go for A.

trainCount.prompt: How many numbers for a row of bells like these?
trainCount.explain: Three: height A, width σ and frequency f. The frequency places every bell at once, however many there are.

trainRate.prompt: Which row has the highest frequency f?
trainRate.explain: The one with three bells every second: f = 3. The height and the width do not change the frequency.

twoBellsCount.prompt: Each beat has a bell up and a bell down. How many numbers do you need?
twoBellsCount.explain: Six: the frequency f, height and width of the first bell (A₁, σ₁), height and width of the second (A₂, σ₂), and the delay d between them.

twoBellsSign.prompt: How does the code say that the second bell points down?

options.negative: Its height A₂ is a negative number
options.flip: We add a number that says "upside down"
options.subtract: The decoder always draws the second bell downwards

twoBellsSign.explain: A negative height does it, with no extra number: the same formula, with A below zero, draws a bell pointing down. (The third answer also works, but then a bell pointing up could never be encoded.)

ecgCount.prompt: One beat is eight bells. Each bell needs its position, width and height, and the heart beats at a certain rate. How many numbers in all?
ecgCount.explain: 8 bells × 3 numbers = 24, plus the heart rate: 25 numbers. A few seconds of ECG are thousands of dots; with this recipe, 25 numbers rebuild them.

ecgTallest.prompt: Which bell has the largest height A?
ecgTallest.explain: R: the sharp spike, when the big chambers of the heart squeeze. S is large too, but negative: it points down.

ecgDecode.prompt: Put the steps to rebuild an ECG from its 25 numbers in order.

steps.read: Read the heart rate and the three numbers of each bell
steps.bells: Draw each of the eight bells at its position, with its height and width
steps.sum: Add the eight bells together, point by point: that is one beat
steps.repeat: Repeat the beat as many times per second as the heart rate says

ecgDecode.explain: It is the same decoder as for one bell, used eight times and then added up, and the same trick as the row of bells to repeat it.

eegHow.prompt: How could we encode this EEG?

options.bells: With a few bells, like the ECG
options.learn: We do not know the recipe: let a computer learn one from many EEGs
options.pixels: We cannot: we must keep every dot

eegHow.explain: Bells and waves can help (the brain does have rhythms, the alpha waves for example), but no fixed recipe of a few shapes rebuilds an EEG well. Keeping every dot works but it is not a code. The modern answer is to learn the recipe from many examples: that is the next step.

vaeCount.prompt: In this autoencoder, how many numbers does the encoder keep from a piece of EEG?
vaeCount.explain: Eight, the column in the middle. We choose how many, as we did for the bells: fewer numbers is a shorter code but a rougher rebuild.

vaeSteps.prompt: Put the steps of a variational autoencoder in order.

steps.encode: The encoder reads a few seconds of EEG
steps.bells: For each of the eight numbers it gives a centre μ and a spread σ: a small bell
steps.draw: A value is picked from each bell
steps.decode: The decoder rebuilds the EEG from those eight values
steps.compare: The rebuilt EEG is compared with the original, and both networks are adjusted to do better next time

vaeSteps.explain: Encode, pick, decode, compare. Repeated on thousands of examples, the comparison is what teaches the two networks the recipe that nobody could write down.

recapMatch.prompt: Drop each picture onto the number of numbers its code needs.
recapMatch.explain: A point on a line 1, on a plane 2, a bell 3, a beat with two bells 6, a heartbeat 25. The pictures get richer, the codes stay short.

recapSteps.prompt: Put the decisions of an encoding in order.

steps.recipe: Choose a recipe: what the pictures are made of
steps.count: Decide how many numbers the recipe needs
steps.encode: Encode: find the values of the numbers for each picture
steps.decode: Decode: rebuild the picture from its numbers, and check that it looks like the original

recapSteps.explain: Recipe, count, encode, decode. When the recipe is unknown, as for the EEG, a neural network learns it.

ball.aria: A ball rolling on a landscape of valleys
ball.hint: Click the landscape to drop the ball somewhere else.

rocking.title: A ball with little friction
rocking.text: The ball keeps its speed for a long time: it rolls back and forth across the shallow valleys before it settles.

stuck.title: A ball with much friction
stuck.text: The ball loses its speed quickly: it stops in the first valley it meets and stays there.

restless.title: A restless ball
restless.text: Now the ball is shaken at random all the time, like the brain's own restless activity. It still spends most of its time in valleys, but now and then a shake carries it over a hill into another one.

soft.title: A soft landscape
soft.text: Now the ground is soft: wherever the ball goes, it digs. The dashed line is the original ground. Watch the valley the ball likes get deeper, and the ball get more and more stuck in it.

wind.title: Neurofeedback: a gentle wind
wind.text: Same soft, restless landscape, but now a gentle wind always blows towards the target valley. It does not carry the ball there: it only makes the moves in that direction a little easier. Over time, the target valley is the one that gets dug.

city.title: A city at night
city.text: Seen from above, a city at night is a pattern of lights that keeps changing: neighbourhoods light up together, then fade, while others come on. Brain activity looks a lot like this.
city.aria: Lights of a city at night, changing in patterns

neuron.title: One neuron, one decision
neuron.body:
An artificial neuron is a very simple machine. It receives a few numbers (its inputs), multiplies each by its own weight, adds them up together with a bias, and then decides: if the sum is above zero it fires (1), otherwise it stays quiet (0).

The weights say how much each input matters; the bias says how easily the neuron fires. With the right numbers, one neuron can already make simple decisions, like the logic gates AND and OR.

biology.title: The neuron in your head
biology.body:
The idea comes from the brain. A biological neuron collects signals from other neurons through its dendrites. Each connection, a synapse, can be strong or weak. The cell body adds up what arrives, and when the total passes a threshold the neuron sends a spike down its axon to the next neurons.

The artificial neuron is a cartoon of this: much simpler, but with the same parts.

line.title: A neuron draws a line
line.body:
Give the neuron the two coordinates of a dot as its inputs. Where is it exactly on the edge between firing and not firing? Where w₁·x + w₂·y + b = 0: that is the equation of a line.

So a neuron splits the plane in two: on one side it fires, on the other it does not. Choosing its three numbers means choosing a line. Try to split the blue dots from the amber ones.

xor.title: The problem a line cannot solve
xor.body:
XOR (exclusive or) fires when exactly one input is on: (0, 1) and (1, 0) yes, (0, 0) and (1, 1) no. Drawn as dots, the two groups sit on opposite corners of the square.

Try as you like: no straight line puts both blue corners on one side and both amber corners on the other. One neuron cannot compute XOR. In 1969 this simple fact slowed down research on neural networks for years.

hidden.title: Add a hidden layer
hidden.body:
The solution is to use more neurons, in layers. Two neurons look at the inputs, each drawing its own line: one computes OR, the other "not both". They are called hidden because nobody sees their output directly. A third neuron looks at the two hidden ones and fires only when both fire.

Together they compute XOR. Each layer turns the problem into an easier one for the next: this is what makes networks with many layers (deep networks) so powerful.

learning.title: Learning from examples
learning.body:
So far we chose the weights by hand. A real network has thousands or millions of weights: nobody can set them. Instead, we give it a dataset: many examples with the right answer (the label), and let it learn.

Learning works like this. The network answers each example, and we measure how wrong it was (the error). Then the error is sent backwards through the network, and every weight is nudged a little in the direction that makes the error smaller. A weight whose input was large gets a bigger nudge; a weight whose input was zero did not contribute, so it does not move. This is backpropagation. Repeat it many times and the weights find their way.

digits.title: Reading handwritten digits
digits.body:
A classic test for neural networks: recognise handwritten digits. Here each digit is a tiny 5 × 7 picture, so 35 pixels go in, one per input neuron. Ten neurons come out, one per digit: the one that fires most is the network's answer.

In between there is a hidden layer of 12 neurons. After training, those 12 numbers are the network's own short description of the picture: it found by itself which features matter to tell a 3 from an 8. Keep this in mind: turning a picture into a few meaningful numbers is exactly what the next module is about.

recap.title: Recap
recap.body: A neuron weighs its inputs and decides. One neuron draws a line; layers of neurons draw any shape. Nobody sets the weights by hand: the network learns them from labelled examples, sending its error back through the layers (backpropagation). And along the way, the hidden layers learn a compact description of what they see.

nnNeuronCount.prompt: How many numbers does this neuron learn?
nnNeuronCount.explain: Three: the weights w₁ and w₂ and the bias b. The inputs are not learned: they come from outside.

nnWhichGate.prompt: A neuron has w₁ = 1, w₂ = 1 and b = -1.5. What does it compute?

options.and: AND: it fires only when both inputs are on
options.or: OR: it fires when at least one input is on

nnWhichGate.explain: With one input on the sum is 1 - 1.5 = -0.5: quiet. With both on it is 2 - 1.5 = 0.5: it fires. That is AND. With b = -0.5 it would be OR.

nnBiology.prompt: Match each part of a biological neuron with its artificial version.
nnBiology.explain: Dendrites bring the inputs, the strength of each synapse is a weight, the cell body computes the sum, and the spike is the output. Learning, in the brain too, mostly means changing the strength of synapses.

nnBias.prompt: What does changing the bias b do to the line?

options.slides: It slides the line without turning it
options.turns: It turns the line around a point
options.colours: It changes which dots are blue

nnBias.explain: The bias slides the line parallel to itself; the weights set its direction. The dots' colours are the labels: they belong to the data, not to the neuron.

nnWhichLine.prompt: Which neuron gets every dot right?
nnWhichLine.explain: The middle one: blue on the shaded side, amber on the other. The last one draws the same line but fires on the wrong side: the sign of the weights decides which side fires.

nnXorBest.prompt: With one line, at best how many of the four XOR corners can you get right?
nnXorBest.explain: Three. Any line that keeps both blue corners together leaves at least one amber corner with them.

nnXorParams.prompt: This network has 2 inputs, 2 hidden neurons and 1 output. How many numbers does it learn?
nnXorParams.explain: Each hidden neuron has 2 weights and 1 bias: 6. The output neuron has 2 weights and 1 bias: 3. In all, 9.

nnHiddenOne.prompt: In the lab above, the first hidden neuron fires for (0, 1), (1, 0) and (1, 1). Which gate is it?
nnHiddenOne.explain: OR: it fires when at least one input is on. The second one is "not both", and the output is the AND of the two.

nnNudgeDown.prompt: The neuron answered 0.9 for a dot whose label is 0, and that dot's x is 1. Which way should w₁ move?
nnNudgeDown.explain: Down. The answer was too high, and w₁ multiplied an input of 1, so it pushed the answer up: lowering it brings the answer towards 0.

nnNudgeZero.prompt: Same mistake, but this dot's x is 0. Which way should w₁ move?
nnNudgeZero.explain: It should not move: an input of 0 times any weight is 0, so w₁ did not contribute to this mistake. Backpropagation gives each weight a share of the error in proportion to what it did. (The bias b still moves.)

nnBackprop.prompt: Put the steps of learning in order.

steps.compare: The answer is compared with the label: that gives the error
steps.back: The error is sent backwards, layer by layer, to every weight
steps.nudge: Each weight moves a little in the direction that makes the error smaller
steps.repeat: Repeat with the next example, many times over the whole dataset

nnBackprop.explain: Answer, compare, send back, nudge, repeat. Each step is tiny; thousands of them make a network that works.

nnDigitParams.prompt: 35 inputs, 12 hidden neurons, 10 outputs. How many numbers does this network learn?
nnDigitParams.explain: Hidden layer: 35 × 12 weights + 12 biases = 432. Output layer: 12 × 10 weights + 10 biases = 130. In all, 562. Networks that read real photos have millions.

nnWhyMany.prompt: Why do we train on many slightly different 3s instead of one perfect 3?

options.shape: So it learns what all 3s have in common, and recognises 3s it has never seen
options.memory: So it can remember every picture by heart
options.faster: Because training is faster with more pictures

nnWhyMany.explain: The goal is to generalise: to recognise new drawings. A network that only memorises its examples fails on the first new one. That is why we test it on digits it has never seen.

nnHiddenCode.prompt: What are the 12 numbers of the hidden layer, for a picture?

options.summary: A short description of the picture that the network invented to do its job
options.copy: A copy of 12 of the pixels

nnHiddenCode.explain: A short description: 35 pixels became 12 numbers that keep what matters to tell digits apart. Nobody told the network what to put there. How to describe something with a few numbers is the subject of the next module, Encoding.

nnRecap.prompt: Put the ideas of this module in the order we met them.

steps.neuron: A neuron weighs its inputs and fires above a threshold
steps.line: One neuron splits the plane with a line
steps.hidden: A hidden layer solves what one line cannot (XOR)
steps.data: A dataset gives many examples with the right answer
steps.learn: Backpropagation nudges every weight to make the error smaller

nnRecap.explain: Neuron, line, hidden layer, dataset, backpropagation: the whole story of neural networks in five steps.

braid.title: Be the signal
braid.body:
Let's start with a game. The network below is a tangle of connections. A signal enters on the left and has to reach the end on the right. At every crossing you choose where it goes next.

There is one rule, and it is the rule of the brain: every time a connection is used, it gets stronger. Here, stronger means thicker, and in the class game a vote on a thick edge counts more. Play several rounds and see what happens.

hebb.title: Neurons that fire together, wire together
hebb.body:
In 1949 the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps another to fire, the connection between them, the synapse, gets stronger. Decades later this was measured in the lab: it is called long-term potentiation. The opposite happens too: connections that are rarely used get weaker, and some are removed.

This is plasticity: the brain changes its own wiring with use. It is what you just did in the game, and it is how we learn, remember, and form habits. A memory is not stored in one place like a file: it is a pattern of stronger connections.

lifespan.title: Plasticity across a lifetime
lifespan.body:
A newborn's brain grows connections at an amazing speed: by the age of two or three a child has many more synapses than an adult. Then, through childhood and adolescence, the brain prunes the connections it does not use and strengthens the ones it does. Some abilities have critical periods, windows when they are learnt most easily: seeing in depth, the sounds of a first language.

The front of the brain, which plans and controls, finishes maturing around the mid-twenties. That is probably where the idea that "the brain stops changing at 25" comes from, but it is wrong: plasticity goes on all life long. Adults who learn to juggle or London taxi drivers who learn the city show measurable changes in their brains. It becomes slower and needs more practice, but it never stops.

The brain even adjusts how plastic it is, depending on its recent activity. This is called metaplasticity, the plasticity of plasticity: a leading idea, still being studied.

habits.title: What it means for us: learning and habits
habits.body:
If use strengthens connections, then what we do again and again shapes our brain. Practice makes a skill automatic; a habit is a route so well dug that we take it without thinking.

How long does that take? In a well-known study (Lally and colleagues, 2010), 96 people picked a new daily habit, such as a glass of water at lunch or a walk after dinner. On average it took about 66 days for the habit to become automatic, but with huge differences: from 18 to 254 days, depending on the person and the habit. The popular "21 days" comes from a 1960 self-help book and is not backed by data. The good news from the same study: missing a single day did not undo the progress.

city.title: The brain at scale
city.body:
Zoom out from single connections to the whole brain. Billions of neurons are active at every moment, and their activity forms patterns that keep moving, like the lights of a city seen from a plane at night.

We can call each pattern a brain state: focused, relaxed, sleepy, anxious, daydreaming. The brain is a dynamical system: at each moment it is in a state, and it moves to the next one. It is like our game, but the nodes are now states and the edges are the transitions between them. How does the brain pick where to go next?

landscape.title: The energy landscape
landscape.body:
A useful picture comes from physics: the energy landscape. Imagine the brain's state as a ball on a landscape of hills and valleys. The ball rolls down the slopes and tends to settle in the valleys. The valleys are the states the brain likes to be in: stable, easy to reach, hard to leave.

Where the ball ends up depends on the shape of the landscape and on where it starts. With little friction it rocks back and forth between a few valleys; with much friction it stays stuck in the first valley it falls into. Try both.

restless.title: A restless brain
restless.body:
A real brain is never still: its activity is noisy, always moving a little at random. So our ball is not a calm ball rolling down: it is a restless ball, shaken all the time.

Most shakes are small and the ball stays in its valley. But sometimes a bigger one carries it over a hill into another valley. Noise is not just a nuisance: it is what lets the brain explore and change state.

soft.title: Plasticity digs the valleys
soft.body:
Now put plasticity into the picture. The landscape is not fixed: it is soft. Every time the ball passes somewhere, the ground there gets a little deeper, like a river that digs its own bed and so carries more and more water along it.

This is how we learn, but it is also how we can get stuck. A state visited again and again (worry, for example) becomes a deep valley that is hard to leave. One leading theory of the brain, predictive coding, says that the brain constantly predicts what will happen and learns from its mistakes; strong predictions can keep us in the same patterns, because we tend to see what we expect. To leave a deep valley, the brain often needs something from outside: a new experience, practice, a push.

wind.title: Neurofeedback: a wind towards a valley
wind.body:
The brain learns from rewards: when something good follows what we did, the chemical dopamine helps strengthen what led to it. For the reward to work, it has to come right away, while the state that earned it is still there.

Neurofeedback uses exactly this. A headband reads your brain activity, and when it moves towards a target state you get an immediate reward: a sound, an image, a video that becomes clearer. It does not force the brain anywhere. It is like a gentle wind that always blows towards one valley: each step in that direction becomes a little easier, and over time that is the valley that gets dug. Exercises and training work in a similar way; research on cognitive reserve suggests that a brain kept active copes better with ageing.

An honest note: the evidence for neurofeedback is promising but mixed, and well-controlled studies are still under way. That is part of why we measure.

demo.title: Your own landscape
demo.body:
Everything in this module comes together in Brain Trails. When you record your EEG with the headband, every few seconds of it are turned into a list of numbers (remember Encoding), and all your recordings are drawn on one map: your Brain Landscape. Its valleys are the states your brain visits most; your trail is the path the ball took.

Neurofeedback in Brain Trails picks a target on your own landscape and rewards every step towards it: the wind of the previous step, blowing on your own map. Let's look at it.

plBraidWhy.prompt: Why did the route get faster and more obvious, round after round?

options.thick: The edges we used got thicker, so they count more and attract the next choices

plBraidWhy.explain: The edges we used got thicker, so the route we took became easier to take again: use strengthens connections, and strong connections get used. In the brain this is how habits form, the good and the bad ones.

plTfContinuous.prompt: True or false: the brain rewires itself all the time.
plTfContinuous.explain: True. Connections are strengthened, weakened, created and removed every day, by everything we do and learn.

plTfUnused.prompt: True or false: connections that are never used tend to weaken.
plTfUnused.explain: True. "Use it or lose it": unused synapses weaken and some are pruned, like the edges that thinned in the game.

plTf25.prompt: True or false: the brain stops rewiring at about 25 years old.
plTf25.explain: False. Around 25 the front of the brain finishes maturing, but plasticity goes on for the whole of life. It gets slower, not absent.

plTfToddler.prompt: True or false: a two-year-old has more synapses than an adult.
plTfToddler.explain: True. The brain first grows far more connections than it needs, then prunes the unused ones through childhood and adolescence.

options.meta: The brain adjusting how easily its connections change, depending on its recent activity

plMeta.explain: Metaplasticity is the plasticity of plasticity: how ready a synapse is to change depends on what it has done recently. It is an active area of research.

plHabitDays.prompt: On average, how long did it take for a new daily habit to become automatic in the study?

options.sixtySix: About 66 days, with big differences between people

plHabitDays.explain: About 66 days on average, from 18 to 254 depending on the person and the habit. "21 days" is a myth.

plTfMissDay.prompt: True or false: missing a single day ruins a new habit.
plTfMissDay.explain: False. In the study, missing one occasion did not really affect how the habit formed. What counts is repeating it most of the time.

plTfRepeat.prompt: True or false: a habit becomes automatic by repeating it in the same situation.
plTfRepeat.explain: True. Doing the same thing in the same context (after breakfast, on the way home) is what makes the route dig in.

plState.prompt: What do we mean by a brain state?

options.pattern: The pattern of activity of the whole brain at one moment
options.region: One region of the brain that switches on

plState.explain: A pattern over the whole brain, like the lights of the whole city at one moment, not one neighbourhood.

plValley.prompt: In the energy landscape, what is a valley?

options.state: A state the brain tends to go to and stay in

plValley.explain: A valley is a state that attracts the brain and holds it for a while: stable, easy to reach, hard to leave.

plTfNoise.prompt: True or false: thanks to its restless noise, the brain can leave a shallow valley by itself.
plTfNoise.explain: True. A bigger shake can carry the ball over a low hill. A deep valley is another story.

plStuck.prompt: The ball is stuck at the bottom of a deep valley. What helps it out?

options.outside: Something from outside: a push, new experiences, practice
options.wait: Waiting: it will leave by itself
options.nothing: Nothing: it is stuck for ever

plStuck.explain: A push from outside. On a soft landscape, waiting only digs the valley deeper. But the landscape is soft for everyone: the same plasticity that dug the valley can dig a new one.

plTfPredict.prompt: True or false: according to predictive coding, the brain is always predicting what will happen next.
plTfPredict.explain: True, according to this leading theory: the brain compares its predictions with what really happens and learns from the difference.

plTfForce.prompt: True or false: neurofeedback pushes the brain into a state by force.
plTfForce.explain: False. It only rewards the brain when it moves in the right direction. The brain does the moving, and the learning.

plReward.prompt: When should the reward come, for the brain to link it to the right state?

options.now: Right away, while the state is still there
options.later: At the end of the session

plReward.explain: Right away. A reward that comes late cannot tell the brain which state earned it. This is why neurofeedback gives feedback within a fraction of a second.

plRecap.prompt: Put the story of this module in order.

steps.use: Use strengthens connections, and what is not used weakens
steps.valleys: Brain states are like valleys of a landscape
steps.stuck: Plasticity digs the valleys we visit, so we can get stuck
steps.nudge: Practice and immediate rewards can gently push us towards new valleys

plRecap.explain: Use, valleys, digging, nudging: plasticity is why we get stuck, and also why we can get out.
